We then plot this result with scripts/josim-plot.py. Install its isolated environment using the Python utility guide, then run:

build/python-utilities/bin/python scripts/josim-plot.py ./ex_jtl_basic.csv -t stacked

This produces the following visualized result:

Through the representation of the results visually, the user can see the two SFQ pulses at the input and through the output resistor, including the phases of the two junctions.

The same process can be done for every example found in the test folder on the repository.

docs.title: Gate-controlled Josephson junctions
docs.text:
Use GC=node to control a junction's critical current with the voltage between that node and ground. The control node must already belong to the circuit.

B1 out 0 junction GC=gate
VG gate 0 DC 5m
.model junction jj(ic=100u, rn=16, r0=160, cap=0.07p, gwidth=10m)

The phenomenological gate model scales the Josephson current by

\[ g(V_g)=\max\left(0,1-\frac{|V_g|}{GWIDTH}\right). \]

GWIDTH is a positive voltage; its default is 0.1 mV. At zero gate voltage the Josephson current is unchanged. It reaches zero at |Vg| >= GWIDTH. The gate does not alter the junction capacitance or resistive branches. This model is a linear suppression approximation, not a microscopic semiconductor junction model.

Gate voltage is interpreted in volts in both analysis modes. In phase mode it is recovered from the node phase using the second-order backward difference. The solver evaluates gate control from the previous solved state, so fast gate transitions require a timestep convergence check.

The earlier experimental ordering B1 out 0 gate junction is also accepted when the model explicitly supplies GWIDTH. Otherwise the extra field retains its legacy WRspice phase-node meaning and is ignored. GC= is recommended because it makes the control explicit. Gate connections are mapped through subcircuit ports and local node names.

For model IV curves, add GTJJ=voltage:

.iv junction 200u iv.csv GTJJ=5m STEP=1u

STEP sets a positive current increment; ISTEP is an alias. The default is 2.5 uA. Each sweep reaches its requested endpoint without overshooting, even when the increment does not divide the maximum current.

TSTEP, TSTOP and TSTART control the model-IV transient and averaging window; the sweep guide explains their limits. Independent slow-RSJ curves verify zero gate, both gate polarities and complete suppression at GWIDTH. For the qualified RN=1mΩ, ICrit=100µA, CAP=0, I=150µA model, the 5 µs protocol gives means within 0.05% of \(R_N\sqrt{I^2-I_{c,\mathrm{eff}}^2}\); finite-window and timestep allowances are derived in the model-IV study.

docs.title: Junction model domains
docs.text:
Model values must be finite. RTYPE is exactly 0 or 1; RN, R0, DELV, ICFCT, GWIDTH and TC are positive. C can be zero. D is in [0,1]. The ordinary sinusoidal model permits signed or zero Ic. The temperature-dependent CPR additionally requires positive Ic and 0<=T<TC. Effective junction area must be positive; an IC override requires a nonzero model Ic. C++ model objects receive the same validation as parsed netlists, including after area/temperature scaling.

At finite positive temperature, D=1 is supported, including the regularized current limit at phase pi. At zero temperature, the fully transparent CPR has a discontinuous cusp. A point numerically at that cusp is rejected; finite positive temperature or a resolved point on either side has a defined value. Arbitrary harmonic/transparency combinations must keep their square-root argument nonnegative throughout the run. See the model-validity study for equations, limits, tolerances and quantitative checks.

The temperature-dependent superconducting expression does not model operation at or above Tc. For a prescribed normal-state RC junction, use RTYPE=0 IC=0 with the chosen RN and C, without enabling that temperature-dependent CPR. Instance TEMP=/global .temp controls thermal noise separately; it does not create a temperature trajectory or automatically switch superconductivity at Tc.

An invalid model or non-finite solved state fails the simulation. Discard a failed run's objects/results; a solver success flag is insufficient on its own.

docs.title: Capacitor voltage (#109)
docs.text:
JoSIM does not implement capacitor IC= or general SPICE initial-condition semantics. Capacitor IC= is rejected explicitly; earlier builds silently ignored it. DST disables negative-time startup and begins with zero stored histories. Default startup advances the circuit from that zero state for a finite settling interval; it does not calculate a DC operating point or set an arbitrary capacitor voltage.

To prepare a nonzero capacitor voltage, include the charging circuit and a long enough charging interval before the event of interest. For example:

V1 IN 0 PWL(0 1m 200p 1m 202p 0 300p 0)
R1 IN OUT 10
C1 OUT 0 1p
.tran 0.1p 300p DST
.print V(IN) V(C1) I(R1) I(C1) I(V1)
.end

Here tau=RC=10 ps. The capacitor charges for 20 tau, then discharges through the resistor after the source falls. The source's finite fall time is part of the physical preparation. This does not instantly assign voltage at t=0 or remove the charging circuit. Use the actual preparation network when it affects other circuit states. A later print-start value can omit preparation from the output while retaining it in the simulation.

The tested netlist is checked against the closed-form RC response in both modes at three steps. See qualification for the equation, error bounds and measurements. Arbitrary initial voltage remains an optional solver feature: a future implementation must initialize the coupled state and all integration histories consistently in both modes and on retries.

docs.title: Stewart–McCumber parameter (#93)
docs.text:
For a sinusoidal RCSJ junction with constant shunt resistance R,

\[ \beta_c=\frac{I_c C R^2}{\sigma},\qquad R=\sqrt{\frac{\beta_c\sigma}{I_c C}},\qquad \sigma=\frac{h}{4\pi e}. \]

R is in ohms, Ic in amperes and C in farads. Use ordinary .param expressions to choose R instead of adding another model field:

.param BETA=1 ICVAL=1u CVAL=0.1p
.param SIGMA_SI={6.62607015e-34/(4*PI*1.602176634e-19)}
.param RSHUNT={SQRT(BETA*SIGMA_SI/(ICVAL*CVAL))}
.model JM JJ(RTYPE=0 IC=ICVAL CAP=CVAL RN=RSHUNT)

This gives R=57.3677591 ohm for beta_c=1. The conversion requires positive, finite beta_c, Ic and C. For C=0, beta_c=0 does not determine R; choose R separately. The complete example is checked through the physical current relation I=Ic*sin(phi)+V/R+C*dV/dt for beta_c=0.2, 1 and 5 in both modes.

RTYPE=0 uses RN as its constant resistance. RTYPE=1 has different subgap, transition and normal-state conductance. It has no single global damping resistance: a beta_c quoted with R0 describes a different operating assumption from one quoted with RN. Gate control, critical-current noise, temperature and a non-sinusoidal CPR can also change the effective damping/stiffness. JoSIM therefore does not accept an ambiguous BETA_C= model parameter. The explicit parameter conversion above is the supported convenience workflow.

docs.title: Current-dependent inductance (#88)
docs.text:
JoSIM's L component is a constant inductance with flux linkage Phi=L*I. Its value expression is evaluated before simulation, not at each timestep. There is no supported L(I) constitutive model or branch-current expression in that value. A static parameter expression does not create a nonlinear element.

For the requested L(I)=L0*(1+a*I^2), the intended meaning must first be chosen:

Meaning of L(I) Flux linkage Phi(I) Differential inductance dPhi/dI Differential inductance in V=L(I)*dI/dt L0(I+aI^3/3), plus initial flux L0(1+aI^2) Flux/current quotient Phi(I)/I L0(I+aI^3), plus initial flux L0(1+3a*I^2)

The factor of three matters. Substituting a time-varying number into the constant-L stamp does not define a consistent nonlinear flux law. A supported implementation would need that law, its derivative, bias/initial flux, mutual coupling semantics, nonlinear solution and convergence tests in both modes.

For a bounded excursion where abs(a*I^2) is small, a constant-L approximation may be sufficient. In the first interpretation, choosing L0 changes the differential inductance by at most 1% when abs(a*I^2)<=0.01 over the entire excursion. This is an element-level bound, not a bound on accumulated circuit phase or amplifier gain. A local small-signal approximation around nonzero bias also needs consistent bias flux. The constant-L limit is covered by analytic RL/RLC regressions; large-signal nonlinear/JTWPA behaviour is outside the current supported model. Full L(I) support remains an optional solver extension.

docs.title: Noise sources
docs.text: JoSIM provides Gaussian white noise and an approximation to power-law noise. Use .option seed=integer to repeat a run in a fresh simulator process. For worked circuits and measured setting choices, see floating flux lines and SQUID noise.

docs.title: White noise
docs.text:
I1 out 0 NOISE(1p 0 1p)

NOISE(ASD TD TSTEP) takes an amplitude spectral density in A/sqrt(Hz) for a current source, or V/sqrt(Hz) for a voltage source. TD defaults to zero. TSTEP sets the noise update interval, denoted by \(\Delta\). If omitted, it is derived from .NEB as 1/(3*NEB). The interval is limited to at least the internal simulation timestep \(h\). The default .NEB is 1 THz; .NEB must be finite and positive. An explicit TSTEP overrides .NEB for that source.

Independent Gaussian values at the update points have variance ASD^2/(2*TSTEP). Values between updates are linearly interpolated. After the initial ramp, the time-averaged one-sided spectrum and total variance are

\[ S(f)=ASD^2\operatorname{sinc}^4(f\Delta),\qquad \overline{\operatorname{var}(x)}=\frac{ASD^2}{3\Delta},\qquad \operatorname{sinc}(z)=\frac{\sin(\pi z)}{\pi z}. \]

Thus the effective bandwidth is \(1/(3\Delta)\), with smooth rolloff rather than a rectangular cutoff. When the timestep floor applies, it becomes \(\min(NEB,1/(3h))\). Older versions used \(\Delta=1/(2NEB)\), giving only two-thirds of the requested time-averaged noise power. This correction changes seeded thermal and omitted-TSTEP white-noise waveforms. Explicit-TSTEP grid variance is preserved, up to rounding. Each junction thermal source is evaluated once per step; a source whose two terminals are ground now advances too, which can change later draws in the process-global stream.

Samples exactly at the update points have variance ASD^2/(2*TSTEP); oversampling approaches the smaller time-averaged variance above. For \(K\) uniformly spaced samples per interval, starting at an update point, the expected sample variance is \(ASD^2(2/3+1/(3K^2))/(2\Delta)\). Setting \(h=\Delta\) therefore does not establish noise accuracy. Resolve circuit dynamics and the interpolated waveform, discard startup, and check timestep refinement. Output sampling and FIR filtering are separate settings: downsampling can alias power outside the output Nyquist band. Keep the seed, bandwidth and sampling choices in the measurement record.

I(source) output uses the samples actually applied by the simulator. Printing does not re-evaluate a noise generator at past times. Source differences and output FIR filtering use the same captured history. Histories are retained only when requested, at about 8 bytes per internal sample per source, plus vector metadata. Output decimation does not reduce that retained internal data.

docs.title: Automatic thermal noise
docs.text:
.TEMP T enables a parallel Norton current source for each resistor and junction. A component's TEMP= overrides the global temperature; TEMP=0 disables its classical noise. Temperatures must be finite and non-negative. Component NEB= overrides the global bandwidth. Both thermal source types use the white-noise interval convention above.

The one-sided current ASD is \(\sqrt{4k_BTG}\). For a resistor, \(G=1/R\). For an RTYPE=1 junction, the active piecewise resistive slope selects

\[ G=\begin{cases} 1/R_0,& |V_{pred}|<V_G-\Delta V/2,\\ I_c/(ICFCT\,\Delta V),& V_G-\Delta V/2\le |V_{pred}|<V_G+\Delta V/2,\\ 1/R_N,& |V_{pred}|\ge V_G+\Delta V/2. \end{cases} \]

RTYPE=0 uses \(1/R_N\) throughout. Here \(V_{pred}\) is the existing explicit voltage predictor used to choose the step's linearization. The current sample uses that step's slope immediately, including on entry to and exit from the transition region. Positive temperature requires positive conductance; zero conductance contributes zero noise.

The resistor relation follows classical equilibrium Johnson–Nyquist noise. Applying it to each junction slope is a local-equilibrium approximation. It does not model quasiparticle shot noise, quantum noise, heating or nonequilibrium gap physics. The transition-region choice is an explicit model assumption, not a microscopic prediction of switching rates. Classical noise also requires relevant frequencies well below \(k_BT/h_{Planck}\).

The Norton source enters node KCL separately. I(R) and I(B) report the constitutive device branch current, excluding its internal noise source. For example, with an ideal voltage source and one noisy junction across the same terminals, -(I(Vdrive)+I(B)) recovers the injected thermal current. There is no separate named trace for an internal thermal source. See the bandwidth and thermal-noise study for measured checks and statistical bounds.

docs.title: Power-law noise
docs.text:
I1 out 0 PNOISE(1p 1 0 1u 1 64)

PNOISE(A1 ALPHA TD TSTEP TCORR N) approximates the one-sided power spectral density A1^2/f^ALPHA, with frequency expressed in Hz. A1 specifies the ideal interior power law's amplitude at 1 Hz, in the source's units per sqrt(Hz). The implementation sums independent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes with logarithmically spaced relaxation times. Finite-band rolloff means the actual PSD at 1 Hz need not equal A1^2 when 1 Hz is near or outside the band.

  • ALPHA is between 0 and 2; 1 gives a 1/f approximation.
  • TD defaults to zero; output before the delay is zero.
  • TSTEP defaults to the simulation timestep and cannot be smaller than it.
  • TCORR defaults to the simulation stop time; zero selects that default.
  • N defaults to 48 and must be an integer from 4 to 512. Increase it when spanning many decades; the minimum count is not an accuracy guarantee.

The nominal band is 1/TCORR to 1/(2*TSTEP). It must have positive width. Its edges have smooth rolloffs, with power outside the nominal band. The total variance therefore differs from the integral of an ideal power law cut off sharply at those edges.

The OU weights follow the power-law integral, including endpoint approximations for the omitted fast/slow tails. Exponents 0 and 2 use the corresponding fast and slow single-pole limits. Exact sampled-OU gain is compensated before linear interpolation. This avoids normalizing to the wrong part of a rolling band edge. It corrects earlier large interior amplitude errors and changes seeded PNOISE/FNOISE/ICNOISE waveforms.

Use frequencies comfortably inside the band and verify refinement for the measurement of interest. With the default 48 processes, the documented analytic scan across 2–8 decades gives less than 2.5% interior PSD error between 10/TCORR and 1/(20*TSTEP), for the tested exponents. A four-process bank can have about 50% interior error over eight decades. Narrow bands may have no well-separated interior at all. These are quantified approximation boundaries, not a rectangular-band filter or a universal error bound.

Changing TSTEP changes the upper turnover frequency and total variance; changing TCORR changes the low-frequency plateau. Moving the entire band by a factor c, at fixed A1, scales variance by c^(1-ALPHA). In particular, 1/f variance is unchanged. Linear interpolation, simulation sampling and output aliasing still matter near the upper edge. See the colored-noise study for the equations, statistical acceptance criteria and controlled-seed measurements.

docs.title: Flux noise
docs.text:
PFLUX loop 0 FNOISE(1u 1 0.25 0 1u 1 64)

FNOISE(A1 ALPHA PHIDC TD TSTEP TCORR N) uses the same process bank. A1 is in flux quanta per sqrt(Hz); PHIDC is a constant flux bias in flux quanta. The returned phase is 2*pi*(PHIDC + noise) radians. The DC bias remains present before TD. Use this source with a circuit representation that relates phase to the applied loop flux; it does not introduce a separate magnetic-field solver.

docs.title: Critical-current fluctuations
docs.text:
B1 out 0 junction ICNOISE=PNOISE(1u 1 0 1u 1 64)

ICNOISE= supplies a dimensionless fractional fluctuation, delta(t), to the Josephson current. The effective critical current is Ic * gate_factor * (1 + delta(t)). Capacitance and shunt resistance are unchanged. Fluctuations below -0.99 are clipped, retaining at least 1% of the nominal critical current before gate suppression. Use small fluctuations when the Gaussian model is intended to represent perturbations about a measured Ic.

The standalone function name ICNOISE(...) has the same arguments and waveform as PNOISE(...). The circuit attribute above also accepts that function name.

docs.title: Runtime and result memory
docs.text:
JoSIM retains every internal sample of each requested primitive trace before formatting or decimating output. A larger print interval reduces the output file, but does not reduce those internal histories.

For effective timestep h and stop time TSTOP, the main double-array payload is

\[ N=\lfloor TSTOP/h\rfloor,\qquad M=8N(1+U+S)\ \text{bytes}, \]

where U is the number of retained matrix-unknown histories and S the number of requested applied-current-source histories. The extra history is time. These counts need not equal the number of displayed columns: a difference can need two operands, while repeated requests can share a primitive. With no explicit trace selection, the default retains all matrix unknowns.

Matrix/solver/device state, custom waveform data, allocator overhead and formatted output add memory beyond this payload. Output conversion can also need working arrays. Timestep retries halve h, increasing the eventual sample count; planning from the requested step alone can underestimate memory.

For example, N=5.1 million with one retained unknown needs about 81.6 MB (77.8 MiB) for time and that unknown alone. Choose duration and requested traces deliberately. Reducing the timestep requires a numerical convergence decision; output decimation cannot substitute for that check.

The simulator reserves the known internal sample count for engaged histories. Unrequested histories remain absent. This avoids repeated growth/copying and reduces measured peak memory, while retaining the existing full-history result API. C++ allocation or vector-size failures produce a recoverable diagnostic with the requested sample count. They cannot catch an operating-system process kill under physical-memory exhaustion; no universal RAM capacity is promised.

The runtime/storage study records the controlled workloads, source identities, wall time, peak resident memory, output comparisons and practical limits. Results depend on circuit, retained traces, toolchain and host; they are not a general throughput specification.

docs.title: Python plotting and phase specifications
docs.text: The maintained postprocessing tools use Python 3.11 or newer. Keep the scripts directory together: the three plotters and the specification generator share input/output checks in plot_common.py. None of these tools needs SciPy. The optional scientific reference tools have their own dependency manifest in the development guide.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From the source checkout, create an isolated environment:

python3 -m venv build/python-utilities
build/python-utilities/bin/python -m pip install -r tools/requirements-utilities.txt

The manifest pins the direct dependencies: NumPy 2.4.1, Pandas 3.0.0, Plotly 7.1.0, Kaleido 1.5.0 and Tabulate 0.10.0. Transitive dependencies are resolved by pip; qualification records their installed versions and wheel hashes. On Windows use build\python-utilities\Scripts\python.exe in place of build/python-utilities/bin/python below.

Interactive plots open in a browser. HTML export embeds Plotly and needs no image renderer. Static image export additionally requires a compatible installed Chrome/Chromium browser, as described by Plotly. Kaleido 1 does not bundle Chrome. BROWSER_PATH can select an installed browser; the tools retain its security sandbox. Browser startup errors fail the export.

docs.title: Plot CSV or DAT output
docs.text:
build/python-utilities/bin/python scripts/josim-plot.py output.csv -x output.html
build/python-utilities/bin/python scripts/josim-plot2.py output.dat \
  -t stacked -j 2pi -c light -o output.png -d 1200x800
build/python-utilities/bin/python scripts/plot-compare.py first.csv second.dat \
  -s 'P(B1)' -x comparison.html
  • .csv uses commas; .dat uses whitespace. The first column is time in seconds; the remaining columns are traces. Samples must be numeric and finite.
  • The single-file plotters offer grid, stacked, combined, square and sep_comb layouts. -s selects trace names exactly as written in the header.
  • josim-plot2.py -j scales phase traces by rad, 0.5pi, pi or 2pi in every layout. Voltage and current traces retain volts and amperes.
  • The comparison plotter uses each file's own time samples. It overlays matching columns from the second file without resampling; first-file traces missing from the second file remain visible on their own.
  • -o supports PNG, JPEG/JPG, WebP, SVG and PDF, including uppercase extensions. EPS export is retired because the supported Kaleido renderer has no EPS output. Use SVG or PDF for vector output.
  • -d WIDTHxHEIGHT requires positive integers. Defaults are 700×500 for the single-file plotters and the existing 3508×2480 for comparisons.
  • Use either -x for HTML or -o for an image. With neither option, the plot opens interactively. Invalid requests and export failures return status 2. Output cannot overwrite either input, including a filesystem alias.

docs.title: Generate a phase-count specification
docs.text:
Provide a CSV containing time followed only by P(junction) phase columns, in radians. Time must be finite and strictly increasing. For example:

build/python-utilities/bin/python scripts/sp_generator.py phases.csv \
  -o phases.sp --start 20e-12 --stability 20e-12 --threshold 0.8

The first sample at or after --start defines each junction's zero-count phase offset. An exact 20 ps sample is unnecessary. For phase displacement \(u=(\phi-\phi_0)/(2\pi)\), the count starts at truncation toward zero; its magnitude increases by one when the remaining fractional magnitude is strictly greater than --threshold. The threshold must lie in [0,1].

A row is written when the complete quantized count vector has remained unchanged for --stability seconds and differs from the last stored vector. The initial zero vector is always written. Reversals and returns toward zero are recorded. Stability uses elapsed time, so nonuniform output grids are supported. Both time options use seconds; zero stability and a start of zero are valid.

This is a sampled phase-count summary. It does not infer events between samples or prove that a physical waveform has settled within a count bin. A final state without enough observed quiet time is omitted. The whitespace-separated SP format retains time and junction-name columns; output cannot overwrite input.

docs.title: Retired preprocessors
docs.text:
noise_insert.py predates native thermal-noise handling. It crashed on blank lines and engineering suffixes, omitted junction-state conductance and used a noise update interval inconsistent with its bandwidth argument. Its entry point now returns status 2, explains the replacement and changes no files.

Use native .TEMP (kelvin) and .NEB (hertz) controls, or component TEMP= and NEB= overrides. Global temperature enables thermal noise in both resistors and junctions; per-component controls permit narrower selection. Remove sources created by the old script before enabling native thermal noise to avoid counting the same resistor noise twice. See noise sources for normalization, timestep limits and the classical physical assumptions.

The old ivcurve.py prototype is also retired. Use the tested model-IV and circuit-sweep workflows.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
build/python-utilities/bin/python -B test/regression_python_utilities.py \
  --report artifacts/python-utilities/report.json

The suite requires a working image renderer. It checks all layouts, phase units, independent comparison timestamps, file preservation, nonuniform phase counts, invalid inputs, three HTML exports and actual exports in every advertised image format. The CI utility job installs a fresh environment and preserves the dependency, browser and test receipts. Release publication requires this job alongside native binary and library qualification. See the qualification study for the measured scope.

docs.title: Floating flux lines and SQUID noise
docs.text: These examples address the floating-reference and noise-setting questions in #107, and external flux and junction thermal noise in #108. They describe classical circuit models; no quantum dynamics are implied.

docs.title: A floating flux line
docs.text:
test/comp/squid_floating_flux.cir couples an electrically separate primary inductor to a two-junction loop. Its voltage source connects two non-ground nodes, which is supported. The entire primary island also needs a voltage reference: without one, its unconstrained common-mode voltage makes the matrix singular. Merely assigning a different node name does not fix that constraint.

RREF REF 0 1g TEMP=0 supplies the numerical reference. In this example it carries zero current, and changing it from 1 ohm to 1 megohm or 1 gigaohm leaves the loop response unchanged. TEMP=0 prevents a global temperature setting from adding spurious noise to this numerical anchor. In a circuit with other paths to ground, the resistor can load a physical mode; verify insensitivity instead of treating it as ideal galvanic isolation.

The signed mutuals are \(-5\) pH and \(+5\) pH, so applied loop flux is \((M_2-M_1)I_P\). A primary current of 51.6958462 uA gives \(0.25\Phi_0\). The independent flux/KCL equilibrium predicts 48.5021253 uA circulating current and junction phases \(\pm0.0485211620\) rad. Both modes, both flux polarities, two timesteps and three reference resistances agree with that prediction. Mutual-inductor signs follow the inductor terminal order in the netlist.

docs.title: A bounded noise example
docs.text:
test/comp/squid_noise.cir uses a symmetric DC-SQUID's zero-loop-inductance limit. Opposite model PHI offsets represent a constant external flux of \(0.25\Phi_0\). This reduction is useful for a checkable noise example; use the coupled finite-inductance circuit above when screening flux and loop inductance matter. A phase-source function does not independently solve magnetic fields.

Each junction has \(I_c=1\) mA, \(R_N=1\) milliohm and \(C=10\) pF. At 1.6 mA total bias the effective parameters give

\[ I_{c,eff}=2I_c\cos(\pi\Phi_{ext}/\Phi_0),\quad R_{eff}=R_N/2,\quad C_{eff}=2C, \qquad \langle V\rangle=R_{eff}\sqrt{I_b^2-I_{c,eff}^2}. \]

The Josephson frequency is 180.946 MHz. The effective plasma frequency is 73.773 GHz, but the very small \(\beta_c=2.15\times10^{-5}\) makes this example strongly overdamped. Its weak classical-noise approximation is checked against 16 seeded runs at each .NEB of 20 MHz, 200 MHz and 2 GHz. The internal step is 2 ps; output spacing is 20 ps without FIR filtering. Discard 100 ns, then measure 5 us. The qualification study gives the independent noise equation, uncertainty and refinement results.

From the repository root, with a built simulator:

build/dev/josim-cli -m 1 -V 1 -a 1 -o build/squid-noise.csv test/comp/squid_noise.cir
python3 -B tools/qualify_squid_noise.py \
  --binary build/dev/josim-cli --output artifacts/squid-noise

The optional scientific owner requires tools/requirements-qualification.txt and a new output directory. It records seeds, the effective timestep, source and binary hashes, per-run PSDs, statistical criteria and a plot. It preserves the input netlists and writes results into its new directory. Native CTest checks the floating-reference example; the longer scientific campaign is a separate qualification command.

docs.title: Choosing settings
docs.text:
• .TEMP enables automatic thermal sources; local TEMP= overrides it. .NEB sets their update interval to max(h,1/(3*NEB)). Local NEB= overrides the global. The noise guide defines variance and rolloff.
  • Resolve the circuit dynamics and noise interpolation with the internal step. Halve that step while holding the physical bandwidth fixed. Setting the step equal to the noise update interval does not establish noise accuracy.
  • Josephson oscillations can mix noise near \(f_J\) down into the measurement band. This example changes noise when bandwidth passes through \(f_J\), even though every tested .NEB is far below its plasma frequency.
  • There is no universal rule that bandwidth must exceed \(f_P\) or \(f_J\). An underdamped plasma resonance, different bias, screening inductance or a different noise mechanism can require different choices. Increase bandwidth and refine the timestep until the intended observable is stable within its statistical uncertainty and model's physical validity.
  • Check output Nyquist frequency and filtering separately. Downsampling can alias unresolved power. Report warmup, duration, sample interval, window, seeds and uncertainty; one noisy trace is not a convergence study.
  • These sources use classical equilibrium/local-slope noise. They do not model quasiparticle shot noise, heating or quantum noise. Relevant noise frequencies must remain well below \(k_BT/h_{Planck}\); that scale is 87.514 GHz at 4.2 K.

docs.title: Parameter sweeps and circuit IV curves
docs.text: .PARAM defines a value for one transient analysis. It does not declare a range or automatically create a Cartesian parameter sweep (#84). Use separate processes for independent points; the supplied helper handles one numeric template marker and an explicit list of values.

docs.title: Five independent resistance points
docs.text:
test/param/sweep_resistance.cir.in defines RX=@VALUE@. A 1 A current source drives RX, giving the independent check \(V=IR\). Run from the repository root:

python3 -B tools/circuit_sweep.py \
  --binary build/dev/josim-cli \
  --template test/param/sweep_resistance.cir.in \
  --values 1,2,3,4,5 --trace 'V(N)' \
  --start 1e-11 --stop 1.8e-11 --output artifacts/resistance-sweep

Values are finite SI numbers; times are seconds. The template can use the marker in a parameter or component expression. The helper replaces its occurrences in the main template and starts a fresh simulator process for each point. --analysis phase selects phase mode; the default is voltage mode.

The output directory must be new. It contains a summary sweep.csv, a JSON report, and each point's effective netlist, log and raw traces. Effective seeds, internal timesteps, computed counts and source/binary/output hashes are recorded. Source templates, includes, custom waveform files and existing result directories are preserved. Relative includes/custom files resolve from the template context. Include/custom filenames must be fixed; continuations must stay within a file.

Remove .FILE and .IV controls when using this isolated workflow. The helper checks reachable includes and rejects those controls before running anything; it does not silently redirect or discard them. Custom files and netlists must remain unchanged throughout the sweep. Simulator errors/timeouts stop the sweep, retain a failed report and witnesses, and never reuse an earlier point's CSV. This helper uses Python's standard library; plotting dependencies are optional.

docs.title: Circuit IV versus model IV
docs.text:
These workflows have different physical histories:

Workflow What is simulated .IV model Imax file STEP=... A built-in single-junction model testbench External fresh-point sweep The complete supplied circuit, restarted at each point One transient with a PWL bias ramp The complete circuit with state carried along that ramp

For an independently checkable circuit example:

python3 -B tools/circuit_sweep.py \
  --binary build/dev/josim-cli \
  --template test/param/sweep_squid_bias.cir.in \
  --values=-0.0002,0,0.0002 --trace 'V(N)' \
  --start 5e-10 --stop 9.9e-10 --output artifacts/squid-iv-sweep

This sweeps the total current through a complete zero-inductance two-junction SQUID at fixed external flux. In the overdamped limit, \(I_c^{eff}=\sqrt2\,100\) uA and \(R_{eff}=8\) ohms. For \(|I_b|>I_c^{eff}\),

\[ \langle V\rangle=\operatorname{sgn}(I_b)R_{eff} \sqrt{I_b^2-(I_c^{eff})^2}. \]

At +/-200 uA the reference is +/-1.13137085 mV. Both analysis modes give +/-1.13153468 mV with the supplied finite measurement window. The 0.015% difference is below the 1% budget, which includes finite endpoint-phase and timestep error. Zero bias gives zero voltage. This example does not imply that fresh points reproduce hysteresis from a continuously swept underdamped circuit.

The mean is a time-weighted trapezoidal integral over the explicit window, with linear interpolation at its boundaries. This handles nonuniform output samples; it does not use row-count averages or extrapolate beyond available data. Choose settling time, duration and timestep for the circuit, and check refinement. A fixed seed in the template reuses a controlled stream at each fresh point; independent noise realizations require explicitly different seeds.

The built-in .IV uses a single-junction transient testbench. Its defaults are 0/10/50 ps bias knots, 0.05 ps initial internal step, 500 ps duration and mean voltage over the second half. Returning branches first visit +/-Imax. Every point starts from fresh zero-state device histories with its specified ramp; it does not carry the preceding point's final state. It does not sweep an arbitrary circuit or provide conventional DC/Newton tolerance control. The generated bias declaration is kept in sync with each point's active source, so a timestep retry retains the requested point rather than restoring a stale testbench current.

Use TSTEP, TSTOP and TSTART to refine the initial internal step, run duration and averaging start, all in seconds. Defaults remain 0.05 ps, 500 ps and half the selected stop time. The averaging start must be at least 50 ps, when the generated source reaches its final bias, and before the stop time. At least two actual averaging samples must remain. The same timing applies to every point. For example, a slow overdamped model can need a much longer plateau:

.model SLOW JJ(RTYPE=0 ICRIT=100u RN=.001 CAP=0)
.iv SLOW 150u slow-iv.csv STEP=150u TSTEP=20p TSTOP=5u TSTART=1u

The mean uses unfiltered internal samples at or after TSTART; the stop time itself is not an extra sample. Timestep retries may reduce TSTEP and never increase it within the curve. -V 1 reports the requested protocol and each point's effective timestep and averaging sample count.

In this example, the Josephson period is about 18.5 ns: the default 500 ps run does not estimate its DC mean accurately. The longer protocol gives 111.7475 nV against the independent RSJ mean 111.8034 nV; halving the step changes it by 0.0002 nV. These are bounded checks, not a universal timing prescription. Refine both timestep and settling/measurement duration for the model. The timestep guard alone does not guarantee accuracy. Use explicit circuit transients for another preparation waveform or continuous hysteresis protocol. See the model-IV study.

The main transient solver uses BDF2 with nonlinear junction terms predicted from prior samples and one sparse linear solve per accepted step. It does not iterate Newton within a step or expose SPICE RELTOL/ABSTOL error control. After the initial 1% of the positive-time grid, a predicted junction phase increment above 0.2 cycles triggers a complete restart at half the internal step. It never increases that step; the final run has a uniform internal grid. This phase-advance guard is not a local truncation-error bound. Explicit timestep and measurement-window convergence checks remain necessary.

docs.title: Retired prototype
docs.text: scripts/ivcurve.py is retired (#82). Its positional netlist edits overwrote existing temporary files, ignored simulator failures and reused stale CSVs. It now exits with an explanation and changes no files. Use .IV for its model testbench purpose, or the fresh circuit workflow above. The qualification study records tests and limits.

docs.title: Syntax Guide
docs.text:
In this section we will attempt to provide the user with a comprehensive guide of the available syntax within JoSIM

JoSIM is CaSe InSeNsItIvE as each line is cast to uppercase upon read-in.

Additionally, it is discouraged to add units to values since in some specific cases this creates confusion in interpretation of the values. An example of this is specifying Farad when assigning a capacitor its value since a value followed by F would be interpreted as Femto. This will lead to wanting a 5 Farad capacitor but receiving a 5 Femto Farad capacitor. Units are not interpreted by the simulator in any way since the component type implies the unit.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
Each line follows similar syntax which uses the first non-blank space character as identifier. Each identifier tells JoSIM how to handle that specific line.

Identifiers that start with a letter relate to physical components in the design, e.g. L, C, R. Lines of this kind almost always follows the same syntax in that it requires a label and two nodes. These nodes can be alphanumeric with the restriction of 0 and GND which indicate a grounded node. Additionally, the use of period (.) or vertical bars (|) in label or node names are prohibited as these are reserved characters within JoSIM.

Only the exact names 0 and GND indicate ground. GNDREF, AGND and other names containing those letters are ordinary nodes. Declared subcircuit pins are bound to their instance connections before physical nodes are classified. A pin named GND can therefore connect to a non-ground node; undeclared ground references inside the subcircuit still refer to global ground.

Lines that start with a period (.) indicate that the line relates in some way to simulation control. In this case the command that follows the period identifies the control, e.g. .tran, .print, .end.

Comments are lines that start with an asterisk (*) or a hash (#). Comments are meant to be in a line of their own and will not work if placed at the end of a line.

Lines that start with a plus sign (+) indicate that the line is a continuation of the previous line. Internally the two lines will be combined.

In most cases the VALUE of a component can be replaced by a variable name or an expression. Variables can be defined using the .PARAM control. These will be discussed in detail further.

Values in JoSIM can be modified with engineering notation or through suffixes. A list of the available suffixes is found below:

Suffix Meaning Engineering Notation Equivalent F Femto 1E-15 P Pico 1E-12 N Nano 1E-9 U Micro 1E-6 M Milli 1E-3 K Kilo 1E3 MEG Mega 1E6 X Mega 1E6 G Giga 1E9 T Tera 1E12

docs.title: Basic Components
docs.text: We will now run through all the available physical components and their limitations. Any parameter surrounded by square brackets are optional and nested square brackets mean that the encapsulated parameter relies on the existence of the previous.

docs.title: Resistor
docs.text:
RLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) VALUE [temp=<TEMP>] [neb=<FREQ>]

The value of a resistor is in Ohms.

Temperature used for noise analysis in Kelvin. Units need to be excluded since K for Kelvin will be interpreted as Kilo by JoSIM, e.g. 4K will become 4000.

Optional neb= sets the thermal-noise effective bandwidth in Hz. The default is 1 THz. The noise guide defines the interpolated spectrum, timestep floor and classical thermal-noise assumptions.

docs.title: Inductor
docs.text:
LLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) VALUE

The value of an inductor is in Henry.

L is constant during simulation; a parameter expression is evaluated once. Current-dependent L(I) is not supported. See the model boundary for flux-linkage semantics and the limits of constant-L approximations.

docs.title: Capacitor
docs.text:
CLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) VALUE

The value of a capacitor is in Farad.

Capacitor IC= is unsupported and produces an error. Prepare a nonzero voltage with an explicit charging interval before measurement. See the tested precharge example.

docs.title: Josephson Junction (JJ)
docs.text:
BLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) <PhaseNode> MODEL [area=<AREA>] [ic=<IC>] [temp=<TEMP>] [neb=<FREQ>]

A Josephson junction has two electrical terminals. An optional third field is normally an unused WRspice phase-node placeholder. A model explicitly specifying GWIDTH can instead use it as a gate, or use the explicit GC=node field. See the gate-controlled junction guide for unambiguous syntax and the physical gate-voltage convention in both modes.

The Josephson junction requires specification of a model name which can be defined anywhere in the program using the control .MODEL.

When AREA or IC is not specified then an area=1 is used as default.

The temp and neb commands have the same descriptions as for the resistor.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
This model control has the following syntax

.MODEL ModelName ModelType([MODEL PARAMETERS])

The only junction model currently supported by JoSIM is the RCSJ model and thus the only available ModelType is jj with the following tunable parameters:

Parameter Range Default Description RTYPE 0, 1 1 Linearization model used VG or VGAP -\(\infty\), \(\infty\) 2.8E-3 Junction gap voltage IC or ICRIT -\(\infty\), \(\infty\) 1E-3 Junction critical current RN 0, \(\infty\) 5 Junction normal resistance R0 0, \(\infty\) 30 Junction subgap resistance C or CAP \(0 \le C < \infty\) 2.5E-12 Junction capacitance T \(0 \le T < T_C\) 4.2 Temperature-dependent CPR temperature in K TC 0, \(\infty\) 9.1 Critical temperature of superconducting material DELV 0, \(\infty\) 0.1E-3 Transitional voltage from subgap to normal D 0.0, 1 0.0 Point of contact transparency affecting current phase relationship ICFCT or ICFACT 0, 1 \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) Ratio of critical current to quasiparticle step height PHI 0, \(2\pi\) 0 Allows phi-junction capability such as the \(\pi\)-junction. CPR {\(-\infty\), \(\infty\)} {1} Sets the Current Phase Relationship harmonic amplitudes. GWIDTH \(0 < GWIDTH < \infty\) 0.1E-3 Gate voltage for complete suppression; enable with GC=node or explicit third-field gate syntax

The .model line belongs to its containing subcircuit. Separate subcircuits can use the same model name. Lookup checks the current instance, its containing instances, then globals. A missing model is an error; it does not select a default model.

For a Stewart–McCumber parameter, use the tested parameter conversion. It defines which resistance enters beta_c; there is no direct BETA_C= field.

All values must be finite. RN/R0/DELV/ICFCT/TC are strictly positive; D is in [0,1]. Temperature-dependent models require positive Ic; ordinary sinusoidal models retain signed/zero Ic support. D=1 uses its finite positive-temperature limit, while the zero-temperature cusp is singular. See model domains for the checked boundaries.

The AREA and IC parameters act as modifiers to the model parameters. AREA is a critical current multiplier, where if IC is specified it replaces the AREA value by \(AREA=\frac{IC_{jj}}{IC_{model}}\).

By setting the PHI parameter of the model, the phase value is persistantly subtracted from the phase (\(\phi\)) in the \(\sin(\phi)\) part of the JJ current. This allows elements such as the \(\pi\)-junction to be modeled.

The CPR parameter alters each individual harmonic of the junction supercurrent. It can either be a singular value or an array of n values encapsulated with curly braces. i.e CPR={0.9, 0.1} to set the current phase relationship to the following \(I = I_C(0.9\sin(\phi) + 0.1\sin(2\phi))\).

docs.title: Transmission Line
docs.text:
TLabel \(N^{+}_{1}\) \(N^{-}_{1}\) \(N^{+}_{2}\) \(N^{-}_{2}\) TD=VALUE Z0=VALUE

TD is the time delay in seconds.

Z0 is the impedance in Ohms.

docs.title: Mutual Inductance
docs.text:
KLabel \(L_{1}\) \(L_{2}\) VALUE

The value is the coupling factor k.

docs.title: Voltage Source
docs.text: VLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) SOURCETYPE

docs.title: Current Source
docs.text: ILabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) SOURCETYPE

docs.title: Phase Source
docs.text: PLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) SOURCETYPE

docs.title: Current controlled current source
docs.text: FLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) \(N^{+}\)Control \(N^{-}\)Control CURRENT GAIN

docs.title: Current controlled voltage source
docs.text: HLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) \(N^{+}\)Control \(N^{-}\)Control TRANSRESISTANCE IN OHMS

docs.title: Voltage controlled current source
docs.text: GLabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) \(N^{+}\)Control \(N^{-}\)Control TRANSCONDUCTANCE IN MHOS

docs.title: Voltage controlled voltage source
docs.text: ELabel \(N^{+}\) \(N^{-}\) \(N^{+}\)Control \(N^{-}\)Control VOLTAGE GAIN

docs.title: Piece Wise Linear (PWL)
docs.text:
pwl(0 0 \(T_{1}\) \(A_{1}\) ... \(T_{n}\) \(A_{n}\))

This source linearly interpolates amplitude values for every time point in the simulation between the specified amplitudes.

Times must be finite, nonnegative and strictly increasing; amplitudes must be finite. The first amplitude can be nonzero. If the first time is positive, JoSIM prepends time zero with that same amplitude and reports a warning. Negative first times are rejected. The final amplitude is held after the last point. PWL returns zero before time zero during startup; PWS holds its first amplitude before the first point.

docs.title: Pulse
docs.text:
pulse(\(A_{1}\) \(A_{2}\) [\(T_{D}\) [\(T_{R}\) [\(T_{F}\) [PW [PER]]]]] )

This source generates a pulse between two amplitudes (\(A_{1}\) and \(A_{2}\)), starts after \(T_{D}\) and has a rise and fall time (\(T_{R}\) & \(T_{F}\)), which default to the transient simulation step size.

PW and PER refer to the pulse width and the period respectively. These values default to the transient simulation stop time when not specified.

Amplitudes must be finite. Delay, rise time, fall time and width must be finite and nonnegative; the period must be finite and strictly positive. Zero rise/fall times give instantaneous edges. Zero width gives a triangular pulse when the edges are nonzero. At each period boundary, the waveform restarts from its rise. At most seven arguments are accepted. Resolve pulse edges and the period with the internal timestep; a finite sampled value does not establish adequate sampling.

docs.title: Sinusoidal
docs.text:
sin(\(A_{O}\) \(A\) [\(f\) [\(T_{D}\) [\(\theta\) [\(\phi\) [\(N_{C}\)]]]]] )

A source that generates a (optionally damped) sinusoidal signal with DC offset \(A_{O}\) and amplitude \(A\) at frequency \(f\) (Hz). If omitted, \(f\) defaults to \(\frac{1}{T_{STOP}}\).

\(T_{D}\) is a start delay: for \(t<T_{D}\) the output is held at \(A_{O}\).

\(\theta\) is an exponential damping factor (units \(s^{-1}\)). When \(\theta=0\), no damping is applied.

\(\phi\) is supplied in degrees and converted internally by \(\phi=\phi_{\deg}\pi/180\).

If \(N_{C}\) is provided and \(N_{C}\) \(>0\), the sinusoid runs for that many cycles and then stops, returning to the offset \(A_{O}\) for all subsequent times.

The function generates a data point for each step in the transient simulation based on the following piecewise definition (let \(\tau=t-T_{D}\)):

\[ f(t)= \begin{cases} A_{O}, & t < T_{D}\\[4pt] A_{O} + A\,e^{-\theta \tau}\,\sin\!\big(2\pi f\,\tau + \phi\big), & T_{D} \le t < T_{D}+\dfrac{\text{$N_{C}$}}{f}\quad(\text{when $N_{C}$}>0)\\[10pt] A_{O}, & t \ge T_{D}+\dfrac{\text{$N_{C}$}}{f}\quad(\text{when $N_{C}$}>0)\\[6pt] A_{O} + A\,e^{-\theta \tau}\,\sin\!\big(2\pi f\,\tau + \phi\big), & t \ge T_{D}\quad(\text{when $N_{C}$}\le 0\ \text{or omitted}) \end{cases} \]

Notes:

  • If \(N_{C}\) is omitted (or \(\le 0\)), the sinusoid continues for the full simulation duration.
  • If \(N_{C}\) \(>0\), \(f\) must be positive to define the stop time.
  • SIN and SINE are aliases. Positive fractional cycle counts specify the corresponding fraction of a period. At the stop time output returns to the offset, including when a nonzero phase makes that return discontinuous.
  • For SINE(0 315u 4g 20p 0 0 4), the stop is 1020 ps. See the finite-cycle qualification.

docs.title: Custom Waveform
docs.text:
cus( wavefile \(T_S\) [SF IM \(T_D\) PER] )

The file contains one line of finite, space-separated amplitude samples. Relative paths use the input netlist's directory, or the current directory for a bare filename or standard input. Samples are multiplied by SF (default 1).

Sample \(k\) occurs at \(T_D+kT_S\). \(T_S\) must be finite and positive; it is not stretched when the simulation uses a coarser step. Choose a simulation step small enough to resolve the input waveform. Before \(T_D\) (default 0), the output is zero.

IM selects a hold (0), linear interpolation (1, default), or a natural cubic spline (2, requiring at least three samples). Linear and cubic methods pass through the stored samples. The last sample is held for one final interval. For \(N\) samples the duration is \(NT_S\): at its end the waveform returns to zero, or repeats from its first sample when PER=1. Repetition is measured from \(T_D\); it does not enforce derivative continuity at a period boundary. PER must be 0 (default) or 1, and \(T_D\) must be finite and non-negative.

docs.title: DC
docs.text:
dc \(A\)

A DC source that is always at \(A\) at any given time during the simulation.

docs.title: Noise
docs.text:
noise(\(A\) \(T_{D}\) \(T_{STEP}\))

The source is zero before \(T_D\). \(A\) is a one-sided amplitude spectral density in A/sqrt(Hz) or V/sqrt(Hz). \(T_{STEP}\) is the Gaussian update interval, limited to at least the internal simulation timestep. If omitted, it is \(1/(3NEB)\) before that floor. The independent values at update points are

\(f(t) = A\frac{GRAND()}{\sqrt{2T_{STEP}}}\)

\(GRAND()\) is a unit-variance Gaussian sample. Values between update points are linearly interpolated, giving time-averaged variance \(A^2/(3T_{STEP})\) and a smooth spectral rolloff. Grid-point variance differs. See the noise guide for sampling and bandwidth conventions.

docs.title: Exponential
docs.text:
exp( \(A_{1}\) \(A_{2}\) \(T_{D1}\) \(\tau_{1}\) \(T_{D2}\) \(\tau_{2}\))

Parameter Default \(T_{D1}\) 0.0 \(T_{D2}\) \(T_{STEP}\) \(\tau_{1}\) \(T_{STEP}\) \(\tau_{2}\) \(T_{STEP}\)

The omitted delay/constant defaults above are independent. In particular, TD2 remains TSTEP when TD1 is supplied. Specify both delays and positive time constants explicitly when preparing a delayed rise/fall waveform.

Returns different values for the 3 different time segments.

For \(t < T_{D1}\):

\(f(t)=A_{1}\)

For \(T_{D1}\le t < T_{D2}\):

\(f(t) = A_{1}+(A_{2}-A_{1})(1-e^{-\frac{t - T_{D1}}{\tau_{1}}})\)

For \(T_{D2} \le t\):

\(f(t) = A_{1}+(A_{2}-A_{1})(1-e^{-\frac{t - T_{D1}}{\tau_{1}}})+(A_{1}-A_{2})(1-e^{-\frac{t - T_{D2}}{\tau_{2}}})\)

docs.title: Piecewise Sinusoidal (PWS)
docs.text:
pws(\(T_{0}\) \(V_{0}\) \(T_{1}\) \(V_{1}\) ... \(T_{N}\) \(V_{N}\) )

A source that generates a smooth, sinusoidally-interpolated waveform through a series of user-defined time/value points, similar to pwl(...) but using a sinusoidal spline between each adjacent pair of points instead of linear interpolation.

Each point is specified as a time/value pair \((T_i, V_i)\). Time values must be strictly increasing.

  • For \(t < T_0\), the output is held at \(V_0\).
  • For \(t \ge T_N\), the output is held at \(V_N\).
  • For \(T_i \le t < T_{i+1}\), the output transitions smoothly from \(V_i\) to \(V_{i+1}\) using a half-cosine (sinusoidal easing) segment.

Let \(u=\dfrac{t-T_i}{T_{i+1}-T_i}\) for the segment \(i\), where \(0 \le u < 1\). The output is:

\[ f(t)=V_i + (V_{i+1}-V_i)\,\frac{1-\cos(\pi u)}{2}, \qquad T_i \le t < T_{i+1} \]

This interpolation is continuous and has zero slope at each specified point, producing smooth joins at breakpoints.

Notes:

  • The final value is held constant after the last timestep \(T_N\).
  • Duplicate or non-increasing time values are invalid and may result in errors.

docs.title: Control Commands
docs.text:
The simulation engine requires control commands to know what to do with the components it has just been provided with.

The most important of these control commands is the transient simulation command as no simulation can be performed without it.

docs.title: Transient Analysis
docs.text:
.tran \(T_{STEP}\) \(T_{STOP}\) [\(P_{START}\) [\(P_{STEP}\) [\(P_{WINDOW}\)]]] DST

For effective step \(h\), JoSIM computes \(N=\lfloor T_{STOP}/h\rfloor\) samples at \(t_k=kh\), \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\). The stop time itself is not an extra sample. Step and stop time must be finite and positive, with at least one supported sample.

\(P_{START}\) selects the first output sample on or after that time. It must not exceed the last computed sample. \(P_{STEP}\) is the print interval. If it is smaller than the requested simulation step, the CLI reduces the initial step to match it. Keep both settings fixed when comparing numerical or noise runs.

If \(P_{WINDOW}\) is specified and not 0, a Hanning FIR filter with a window width of \(P_{WINDOW}\) seconds is applied to the output data before decimating as a post-processing step. This can be used to low-pass filter the output to prevent aliasing when decimating with \(P_{STEP}\), e. g. to create an IV curve of the whole circuit.

Print targets are \(P_{START}+nP_{STEP}\), selecting the first available internal sample at or after each target. A few floating-point ulps at an exact grid tie are treated as equal. Integer step ratios therefore retain a uniform print grid without accumulated rounding jitter. A fractional ratio generally selects nonuniform internal samples; use the recorded timestamps for such data. Verbose mode (-V 1 or higher) reports the effective internal timestep and computed sample count after any full-run timestep reduction.

The FIR window must be finite and non-negative; widths longer than the run are clamped to its duration. An output window containing no computed samples is an error, including when \(P_{START}<T_{STOP}\) but lies after the last grid point.

DST disables the start-up time. The start-up time is a period calculated internally by the simulator in which components settle. This is equivalent to the few picoseconds from when a circuit initially receives power (power switch flipped).

docs.title: Subcircuits
docs.text:
Subcircuits allow subdivision and reuse of smaller circuits within a larger design. When wrapped in a subcircuit control devices are allowed to have the same label names as specified elsewhere in the netlist as the subcircuit completely isolates them.

Subcircuits have the following wrapping control syntax

.subckt SubcktName IO Nodes

...

.ends

The SubcktName specifies the name of the subcircuit and IO Nodes specify the which nodes within the subcircuit connects to outside.

A subcircuit can be used in the main netlist or another subcircuit (nesting) using the following syntax

XLabel SubcktName IO Nodes (JSIM mode)

XLabel IO Nodes SubcktName (WRspice (normal SPICE) mode)

Named parameters can be supplied on each instance, with optional defaults in its .subckt header. PARAMS: is optional. Spaces around = and expressions in braces are accepted.

.param BASE=10
X1 CELL A 0 RES={BASE*2}
X2 B 0 CELL RES=5
I1 0 A 1
I2 0 B 1
.subckt CELL IN RET PARAMS: RES=10 SCALE=2
.param TOTAL=RES*SCALE
R1 IN RET TOTAL
.ends

The two resistances are 40 ohm and 10 ohm. An instance override is evaluated in the caller's environment before binding the child; RES={RES*2} uses the caller's RES. Other assignments on the same instance are not visible while its override expressions are evaluated. The child's defaults and local .param expressions then resolve using the bound values. Lookup proceeds from that instance through its containing instances to global parameters. Local names shadow inherited names; each instance remains independent. Undefined names and parameter dependency cycles fail with a parsing diagnostic.

An override can introduce a local name without a header default, as in X1 CELL A 0 RES=10 with R1 IN RET RES in CELL. Prefer explicit defaults when a reusable circuit has a useful default value. Numeric local definitions are evaluated when instantiated or requested by a model IV command. Structural subcircuit cycles and unknown child types are rejected even in unused definitions.

Legacy component-label overrides also remain available: X1 CELL A 0 R1=5 replaces the value of resistor R1. A nested label uses inside-to-outside order, such as R1|XCH=5. This applies to R/L/C/K values, E/F/G/H gains, T delay, and an existing B AREA= or IC= assignment. An explicitly declared parameter of the same name takes precedence over this legacy shortcut. Duplicate assignments on one header or instance are errors; a later separate .param declaration replaces an earlier expression with a warning.

Local JJ models are evaluated separately for each instance. Model lookup checks that instance, then containing instances, then globals. A local model always shadows a global model of the same name. Parameter values are never substituted into node names, filenames or model identifiers.

docs.title: Noise
docs.text:
As mentioned in the technical discussion, noise can be automatically inserted as current sources in parallel to each resistor. This thermal noise temperature and bandwidth can be specified globally using the following commands:

.temp Temperature in Kelvin

.neb Bandwidth in Hertz

Temperature must be finite and non-negative; bandwidth must be finite and positive. Local TEMP=/NEB= settings override the globals. TEMP=0 disables classical thermal noise for that component. The default bandwidth is 1 THz. Junction thermal noise uses the active resistive slope, with the explicit local-equilibrium limits described in the noise guide.

docs.title: Spread
docs.text:
JoSIM allows each value of inductors, resistors, capacitors and JJ (area/Ic) to be spread uniformly within a specified percentage range from the nominal value. Each time the value is used (in matrix creation), a new random value from the uniform distribution is chosen.

This allows for process variation to be simulated.

To set the spread globally, the following control needs to be set:

.spread Normalized percentage [L=Inductor spread] [B=JJ spread] [C=Capacitor spread] [R=Resistor spread]

Each individual component can also be spread by adding the spread= named parameter to the component declaration line.

The order of precedence is taken as local, specific global and then global. This means that if a global spread exists but a global inductor specific spread also exists and the inductor being added has a local spread then the local spread will take precedence.

An example:

If an inductor has a value of 2pH, this is its nominal value. If a local spread of 0.2 is specified this means a random value can be chosen anywhere between 1.6pH and 2.4pH. If global inductor specific spread is specified as 0.3 and the local spread is not defined, the value can be anything within the range 1.4pH - 2.6pH. Similarly if the global spread is defined as 0.5 then the value each time the simulation is run can be anywhere between 1pH and 3pH.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
For both noise and spread a random number generator is seeded upon creation of the input object. This is done to enable non-deterministic noise/spread. However, in some cases the user might wish to produce deterministic noise/spread between runs. To enable this a .option seed= has been added. An integer seed value can be specified to obtain deterministic noise/spread. Additionally, the current auto-seeded run's seed can be obtained using verbose mode (-V 1).

An example: 

.option seed=4190754512324517577

docs.title: IV Curve
docs.text:
JoSIM allows the user to output an IV curve for a specified JJ model within the netlist using the following command:

.iv modelname max_current filepath [STEP=current] [GTJJ=voltage] [TSTEP=time] [TSTOP=time] [TSTART=time]

This command outputs a comma seperated value (CSV) at the filepath specified which contains the IV curve data for the modelname from negative max_current to positive max_current.

Subcircuit models can be output using . or | between the model name and subcircuit definition name, for example .iv JM.CELL 350u iv.csv STEP=175u. This evaluates the definition's default parameters with global fallback. It uses no particular instance's overrides or caller environment; missing required defaults are errors. This command draws a model IV curve, rather than sweeping an arbitrary connected circuit.

STEP (alias ISTEP) is the positive current increment, default 2.5 µA. GTJJ supplies a physical gate voltage. TSTEP selects the initial internal step (default 0.05 ps), TSTOP the duration (default 500 ps), and TSTART the averaging start (default half the selected duration). Timing values use seconds and engineering suffixes. Require TSTEP > 0 and TSTOP > TSTART >= 50 ps, with at least two actual averaging samples. Every point starts with fresh device histories and its specified 0/10/50 ps bias ramp. The mean uses unfiltered internal samples from TSTART; retries may reduce the step. -V 1 reports the effective grid. These finite transients require model-specific settling and convergence checks; see model IV versus circuit sweeps.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
A simulation is meaningless unless the results are post processed. In order to know which of these results are relevant for storage the simulator needs output control commands.

These output commands can be of either

.print .plot .save

Any of these commands can be followed by either of the following commands

PrintType Device or Node

PType(Device or Node)\(_0\) ... PType(Device or Node)\(_n\)

Where PrintType can be either device voltage (DEVV), device current (DEVI), device phase (PHASE), node voltage (NODEV) or node phase (NODEP).

When specifying a device type store only a single device can be specified, but when a node type store is specified 2 nodes can be specified to store the difference between them.

PType is shorthand for the above and can have multiple per line requests. PType can be either of V, I (or C) or P followed by the device or node in brackets. If more than one device or node is specified by comma seperation (maximum 2) the difference between the two devices or nodes is stored.

An additional save type exists that has the following syntax

@Device[PType]

This stores the PType of the device specified.

Subcircuit parameters can be output using the .(period) or |(vertical bar) as separator between the device label and the subcircuit label name.

i.e. .print v(14.X01) p(B01.X02)

This method follows the path from inside to out when nested subcircuits are used.

Declared pin aliases are supported as well as internal nodes and components. For example, V(IN.X1) addresses pin IN of instance X1, and V(IN.X2.X1) addresses its nested instance X2. Ground pins produce a zero trace when connected to ground. V(0,N) is the negative of V(N).

Unknown devices, nodes, aliases and malformed output requests are errors. Requested traces are never silently discarded. C(R1) is an alias for I(R1). Device differences such as V(R1,R3), P(B1,B2) and I(R1,R3) subtract the two physical traces after applying the same output sampling/filter. General arithmetic expressions over output vectors remain unsupported.

Subcircuits as mentioned before can also be nested almost indefinitely as they are expanded upon simulation.

If the label is not immediately apparent and required for output, the simulation can be run using the -V 3 cli option to show the expanded main design, allowing the exact label name to be identified.

docs.title: File
docs.text:
Multi-file output can be achieved by separating output commands with the following command:

.file filepath

This indicates that every output request that follows this command needs to be stored in the file specified by filepath.

I.e. 

.file output1.csv
.print p(B1) p(B2) p(B3)
.file output2.dat
.plot i(L01) i(L02) i(L03)
.file output3
.save v(1) v(2) v(3)

This will create 3 output files. The first will be a CSV file containing only the phase outputs. The second file will be a space separated file containing only the currents. Lastly, the third file will be in a SPICE RAW format and contain only the voltages.

The use of this command does not affect the command line option request to output a file. The command line output option, if requested, will output an additional file which contains all of the output requests (phase, current and voltage).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
The final control command that is of importance in JoSIM is the parameters command with the following syntax

.param VarName=Expression

VarName is the variable name that can be used anywhere else in the circuit and Expression is a mathematical expression that is evaluated using an implementation of Dijkstra's shunting yard algorithm, whereby the expression is converted into reverse polish notation (RPN) and evaluated.

Additionally, expressions can also contain other variables and parameters will be continuously evaluated until all variables are reduced to values. If variables are not defined the program will halt and produce an error.

Numeric literals support decimal/scientific notation (1E-3, 1e-3, 1.E-3) and case-insensitive SPICE engineering suffixes. M or m means milli; MEG means mega. The remaining suffixes are T, G, K, U, N, P and F. ASCII unit labels may follow a suffix, such as 2mV.

Expressions support +, -, *, /, ^, matching (), [] or {}, unary signs, and the documented mathematical functions. Exponentiation is right associative and precedes a leading unary sign: 2^3^2 is 512, -2^2 is -4, and 2^-3 is 0.125. Function calls bind before a following power. LOG is the natural logarithm and LOG10 is base ten. Evaluated expressions must produce finite real values; missing operands, invalid function arguments and mismatched brackets produce parsing errors.

Parameter expressions resolve local names first and then global names for every operand. Undefined names and dependency cycles fail with a diagnostic. Component and source parsers that accept parameter expressions use the same evaluator; when an expression contains spaces, define it with .param and use its name so that component fields remain unambiguous. Hierarchical named overrides are tracked separately in the audit-resolution ledger.

docs.title: Control Block
docs.text:
Any of the above controls can be wrapped inside a control block with the following syntax

.control

...

.endc

Wherein all controls can be specified by omitting the usual prepending .(period) to the command.

This block, though seemingly useless at present, will be used for more advanced functionality in the future.

docs.title: Include
docs.text:
JoSIM allows the use of a .include control card that uses the following syntax

.include relative_path_to_file

This command reads in the contents of the relevant file pointed to by the relevant path upon parsing of the netlist essentially extending the netlist by the linked file. This is incredibly handy when large subcircuits are involved and reuse of subcircuits across multiple files is required.

This can also be used to house all the models used in simulation allowing a central point of alteration if the model is changed.

docs.title: Standard Input
docs.text: JoSIM now allows input from standard input allowing a line-by-line read in of a netlist until the .end card is found or alternatively the EOF character is returned.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
JoSIM has a set of built in constants that when used expand to the corresponding values. Below is a list of these constants and their values. The constants names are case insensitive:

Constant Symbol Value PI \(\pi\) 3.141592653589793238463 PHI_ZERO \(\Phi_{0}\) 2.067833831170082E-15 BOLTZMANN \(k_{B}\) 1.38064852E-23 EV \(e\) 1.6021766208E-19 HBAR \(\bar{h}\) 1.0545718001391127E-34 C \(c\) 299792458 MU0 \(\mu_{0}\) 12.566370614E-7 EPS0 \(\epsilon_{0}\) 8.854187817E-12 SIGMA \(\sigma\) (short for \(\frac{\Phi_{0}}{2\pi}\)) 3.291059757E-16
